name: Purple coneflower
wildlife: Bees, butterflies; goldfinches eat the seed
notes: Tough, long-blooming prairie classic. Leave the seed heads standing for birds.

name: Pale purple coneflower
notes: Missouri prairie native with a deep taproot. Very drought tolerant once established.

name: Ozark (yellow) coneflower
notes: The only yellow Echinacea, found wild almost nowhere but the Missouri Ozarks.

name: Orange coneflower / black-eyed Susan
notes: Spreads into bold drifts. Annual black-eyed Susan (R. hirta) is shorter-lived but reseeds.

name: Butterfly milkweed
wildlife: Monarch caterpillar host; nectar for many butterflies
notes: Needs good drainage (avoid wet clay) and resents moving. Slow to emerge in spring, so mark it.

name: Swamp milkweed
notes: The milkweed for heavy clay and low, wet spots; it isn't aggressive.

name: Aromatic aster
wildlife: Late-season nectar for bees and migrating monarchs
notes: Mounding and tidy; 'Raydon's Favorite' is a popular form. Give it a spring haircut in late April for a compact plant.

name: New England aster
notes: Tall; cut back by half in late April–early May so it doesn't flop.

name: Wild bergamot (bee balm)
notes: Minty leaves deer avoid; spreads moderately. Some powdery mildew in late summer is normal.

name: Missouri evening primrose
notes: Sprawling front-of-border plant for hot, well-drained spots and rock walls; rots in wet clay.

name: Prairie blazing star
notes: Tolerates heavy clay. Rabbits and voles like the corms.

name: Rattlesnake master
notes: Architectural, yucca-like leaves; a striking prairie accent.

name: Foxglove beardtongue
notes: Early-summer bloom that fills the gap between spring bulbs and summer prairie flowers.

name: Blue false indigo
notes: Shrub-sized, long-lived and fixes its own nitrogen; don't move it once planted.

name: Lanceleaf coreopsis
notes: Cheerful, drought-proof; deadhead for rebloom.

name: Culver's root
notes: An elegant vertical accent for the back of the border.

name: Sweet Joe Pye weed
notes: Big back-of-border plant for moist clay; a spring haircut keeps it shorter.

name: Great blue lobelia
notes: Late color for moist, part-shade spots; short-lived but reseeds.

name: Cardinal flower
notes: Wants consistently moist soil, such as a rain garden or near a downspout.

name: Wild columbine
notes: Dainty woodland plant; reseeds in well-drained spots.

name: Wild geranium
notes: Spring woodland groundcover under trees.

name: Virginia bluebells
notes: Spring ephemeral: blooms, then goes dormant by June. Pair it with hostas or ferns.

name: Stiff goldenrod
notes: Goldenrod doesn't cause hay fever (ragweed does). This one is clump-forming, not a runner.

name: Royal catchfly
notes: A rare Missouri prairie plant. Grow Native! nurseries sometimes carry it.

name: Ohio spiderwort
notes: Flowers open in the morning; cut back after bloom for fresh leaves.

name: Eastern bluestar
notes: Soft blue spring stars and golden fall foliage; long-lived and trouble-free.

name: Little bluestem
wildlife: Host for skipper butterflies; winter cover
notes: The signature Missouri prairie grass. Gets floppy if over-watered or over-fed.

name: Prairie dropseed
color: Fine green mounds, gold in fall
notes: Fine-textured fountain; the seed heads smell like popcorn. A great edging grass.

name: Switchgrass
color: Airy seed plumes; red or blue cultivars
wildlife: Winter cover and seed for birds
notes: Adaptable screen or backdrop ('Northwind' stays upright).

name: Pennsylvania sedge
notes: A soft, grass-like lawn alternative for dry shade under trees where fescue fails.

name: Wild ginger
notes: Heart-shaped leaves form a dense shade groundcover.

name: Golden groundsel
notes: Semi-evergreen groundcover that spreads well in moist shade.

name: Fragrant sumac 'Gro-Low'
color: Tiny yellow flowers; orange-red fall color
notes: The go-to for slopes and a replacement for burning bush or spreading junipers.

name: Ninebark
color: White flowers; burgundy or gold leaves in cultivars
notes: Tough and fast. Prune the oldest stems right after flowering.

name: Smooth hydrangea ('Annabelle')
notes: Missouri native; blooms on new wood, so cut it back hard in late winter. It wilts in afternoon heat but recovers.

name: Virginia sweetspire
notes: Handles wet clay; 'Henry's Garnet' is the common form. Spreads slowly by suckers.

name: Buttonbush
notes: For rain gardens and soggy spots.

name: Spicebush
color: Yellow flowers in March; red berries; gold fall color
notes: An excellent native replacement for bush honeysuckle in shady yards.

name: New Jersey tea
notes: Deep-rooted, drought-proof prairie shrub; needs good drainage.

name: American beautyberry
notes: Native to southern Missouri; may die back in hard KC winters but regrows and blooms on new wood.

name: Oakleaf hydrangea
color: White panicles aging pink; red fall leaves
notes: Southeastern native that does well in KC shade with decent drainage. Blooms on old wood, so prune lightly right after flowering.

name: Panicle hydrangea ('Limelight', 'Bobo')
notes: The most reliable hydrangea in KC clay and sun. Blooms on new wood; prune in late winter.

name: Shrub roses (Knock Out types)
notes: Easy bloomers, but rose rosette disease is common locally; remove infected plants. Don't mass-plant them.

name: Daylily
notes: Nearly indestructible on clay. Avoid the orange "ditch lily," which escapes into roadsides.

name: Hosta
notes: Shade workhorse, but deer and rabbit candy. Blue and thick-leaved types handle heat and slugs best.

name: Sedum 'Autumn Joy'
notes: Drought-proof; flops in rich or wet soil, so pinch it back in early June.

name: Russian sage
notes: Loves heat and poor, dry soil; cut to 12 in when new growth appears in spring.

name: Catmint 'Walker's Low'
notes: Shear it by half after the first flush for a second bloom.

name: Meadow sage 'May Night'
notes: Deadhead for repeat bloom through summer.

name: Eastern redbud
notes: The Missouri spring signature, and the cue for crabgrass preventer. Short-lived (20–30 yrs); avoid herbicide drift near it.

name: Serviceberry
notes: Four-season small tree and a great Callery pear replacement.

name: Swamp white oak
wildlife: Hosts hundreds of caterpillar species that songbirds feed on
notes: Handles wet clay and compaction; one of the best shade trees for KC yards.

name: Bur oak
notes: Drought-tough prairie oak; plant for your grandchildren. Prune only in winter (oak wilt).

name: Blackgum (tupelo)
notes: Slow but very long-lived; tolerates wet clay.

name: Kentucky coffeetree
notes: Tough urban shade tree for clay, drought and road salt; choose seedless male cultivars ('Espresso').

name: American hornbeam
notes: Smooth "musclewood" bark; an understory tree for shady yards.

name: Flowering dogwood
notes: Missouri's state tree, but it struggles in hot, exposed sites and heavy clay. Give it afternoon shade and good drainage.
